question: What is the main goal of a Drug Revolving Fund (DRF) in a hospital?

options.A: To ensure a continuous supply of affordable essential drugs
options.B: To provide free medical care to all indigent citizens
options.C: To fund the construction of new hospital wards and buildings
options.D: To generate heavy profits for the hospital management board

explanation: Think of the DRF as a self-sustaining cycle. Its main job is to make sure essential drugs never run out in the hospital pharmacy, so patients can always get what they need at a fair price! [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h1)

question: How does the 'revolving' part of a DRF actually work in practice?

options.A: Unsold expired drugs are returned to manufacturers for full cash refunds
options.B: Donors inject new capital into the pharmacy every single month
options.C: Money collected from drug sales is used to buy fresh stock
options.D: Profits from drug sales are returned to the government treasury

explanation: Spot on! Patients buy drugs, that money goes back into the kitty, and the pharmacy uses it to buy the next batch. It is a continuous loop that keeps the pharmacy stocked. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h1)

question: Which of these is NOT a core principle of a Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: Maintaining strict financial accountability and transparency
options.B: Selling pharmaceuticals at affordable prices to patients
options.C: Maximizing high profit margins for hospital expansion
options.D: Ensuring constant availability of essential medicines

explanation: A DRF is not a business meant to chase huge profits! It focuses on cost-recovery to keep medicines affordable and available for everyday patients. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h2)

question: Why is quality checks a must-do when buying drugs for the DRF?

options.A: To allow the hospital to charge higher prices for branded items
options.B: To prevent substandard or fake medications from harming patients
options.C: To ensure that expired drugs can be easily hidden from auditors
options.D: To make certain that foreign drugs are favored over local ones

explanation: Patient safety comes first! Checking drug quality ensures that fake or substandard medicines never reach the people trusted in our care. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h2)

question: Who usually sits on the management committee for a hospital's Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: Elected political leaders from the local government council
options.B: Only senior nursing officers working in the surgical ward
options.C: A multidisciplinary team including pharmacists and accountants
options.D: Only external auditors and private business investors

explanation: It takes teamwork! Managing a DRF needs a mix of clinical, pharmaceutical, and financial experts to keep everything running smoothly and transparently. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h3)

question: What happens to a DRF if hospital staff constantly collect drugs on credit and fail to pay back?

options.A: The suppliers will double the credit period for future orders
options.B: The pharmacy will automatically start generating higher profits
options.C: The fund will quickly experience cash depletion and stockouts
options.D: The government will automatically inject fresh emergency funds

explanation: Unpaid credit creates holes in the system. If the cash doesn't come back in, the pharmacy won't have money to buy new medicines when patients need them. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h3)

question: Why do DRF programs love buying drugs by their generic names?

options.A: Patients refuse to take medications with brand names
options.B: Generic drugs do not require any regulatory inspection
options.C: Generic drugs are much cheaper than branded equivalents
options.D: Generic medications never expire on hospital pharmacy shelves

explanation: Generic drugs give us the same medical power as expensive brand names, but at a much lower cost—helping keep healthcare affordable for everyone. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why is proper cold chain storage a big deal in the DRF supply chain?

options.A: To ensure that large bulk orders take up less physical warehouse space
options.B: To speed up the delivery time from the manufacturer to the hospital
options.C: To comply with tax laws regarding imported pharmaceutical goods
options.D: To prevent temperature-sensitive medications like vaccines from losing potency

explanation: Some medications (like vaccines and insulin) are fragile. If they get too warm, they lose their strength and won't work for the patient. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h4)

question: What does 'ring-fencing' mean when managing DRF finances?

options.A: Selling medications only to patients with valid health insurance
options.B: Building a physical fence around the hospital pharmacy store
options.C: Protecting DRF funds so they are only used to buy drugs
options.D: Insuring all drug shipments against theft and fire damage

explanation: Ring-fencing is like putting a protective bubble around the drug money so nobody can borrow it for other hospital bills, keeping the revolving cycle alive! [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h5)

question: If a hospital uses all its DRF cash to fix a broken generator, what happens first?

options.A: The hospital will immediately receive a large grant from the ministry
options.B: Patients will start buying cheaper drugs from the hospital store
options.C: The cost of electricity in the wards will drop significantly
options.D: The pharmacy will soon run out of money to restock essential drugs

explanation: That breaks the rule of ring-fencing! Without cash in the revolving account, new medicine orders can't be placed, leading straight to empty shelves. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h5)

question: How do nurses directly help make a hospital Drug Revolving Fund successful?

options.A: By auditing the central bank accounts of the hospital management
options.B: By setting the retail profit markups for all essential medicines
options.C: By importing foreign pharmaceuticals directly from overseas factories
options.D: By providing feedback on drug stock levels and ward consumption

explanation: As nurses, we work directly with patients and medications every day. Spotting low stock early and letting pharmacy know helps keep the supply chain smooth. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h6)

question: Why is it important for nurses to help manage emergency drug supplies on the ward?

options.A: It removes the need for any professional pharmacist involvement
options.B: It ensures drugs are tracked, accounted for, and properly replenished
options.C: It guarantees that all ward drugs will be distributed completely free
options.D: It allows nurses to sell medications directly to patients for personal profit

explanation: Good ward management stops drugs from wasting, expiring, or disappearing without a trace, keeping the whole revolving fund healthy. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is a major economic headache for the long-term capital of a DRF?

options.A: High rates of national inflation eroding purchasing power
options.B: Strict adherence to quality assurance during procurement
options.C: An excessive surplus of cash sitting in the pharmacy safe
options.D: Too many patients buying generic drugs instead of brands

explanation: When inflation hits hard, prices shoot up. The same amount of cash buys fewer and fewer drugs over time, making it tough to keep shelves full. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h7)

question: Why does giving out too much informal credit to patients hurt a DRF?

options.A: It encourages manufacturers to stop producing generic medicines
options.B: It causes all the drugs in the pharmacy warehouse to expire faster
options.C: It forces the government to increase taxes on medical supplies
options.D: It creates cash flow gaps that prevent timely restocking of medicines

explanation: When money is stuck as 'owed bills', the pharmacy drawers are empty. Without cash on hand, suppliers won't send new stock. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h7)

question: What is the main reason for doing routine physical stock counts in a pharmacy?

options.A: To compare actual physical inventory with financial records
options.B: To calculate the annual salary bonus for the nursing staff
options.C: To return all expired items directly to government ministers
options.D: To increase the retail price of all fast-moving medications

explanation: Stock counts help catch errors, missing items, or record mistakes early, making sure the physical drugs match what the books say. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h8)

question: If a hospital notices that drugs are sitting too long and expiring on the shelf, what should they do?

options.A: Stop all auditing procedures to save time and administrative money
options.B: Double the selling prices of all remaining stock to make up for losses
options.C: Force ward nurses to purchase the expired drugs for personal use
options.D: Review ordering patterns to buy smaller, more appropriate quantities

explanation: Expiring stock means they are ordering more than patients actually need. Adjusting the order size stops valuable medicine from going to waste! [learn more](GNS215_U3_T1#GNS215_U3_T1_h8)
